CHAPTER XIV.


The sudden termination of Colonel Brandon’s visit at the park, with his
steadiness in concealing its cause, filled the mind, and raised the
wonder of Mrs. Jennings for two or three days; she was a great
wonderer, as every one must be who takes a very lively interest in all
the comings and goings of all their acquaintance. She wondered, with
little intermission what could be the reason of it; was sure there must
be some bad news, and thought over every kind of distress that could
have befallen him, with a fixed determination that he should not escape
them all.

“Something very melancholy must be the matter, I am sure,” said she. “I
could see it in his face. Poor man! I am afraid his circumstances may
be bad. The estate at Delaford was never reckoned more than two
thousand a year, and his brother left everything sadly involved. I do
think he must have been sent for about money matters, for what else can
it be? I wonder whether it is so. I would give anything to know the
truth of it. Perhaps it is about Miss Williams and, by the bye, I dare
say it is, because he looked so conscious when I mentioned her. May be
she is ill in town; nothing in the world more likely, for I have a
notion she is always rather sickly. I would lay any wager it is about
Miss Williams. It is not so very likely he should be distressed in his
circumstances _now_, for he is a very prudent man, and to be sure must
have cleared the estate by this time. I wonder what it can be! May be
his sister is worse at Avignon, and has sent for him over. His setting
off in such a hurry seems very like it. Well, I wish him out of all his
trouble with all my heart, and a good wife into the bargain.”

So wondered, so talked Mrs. Jennings. Her opinion varying with every
fresh conjecture, and all seeming equally probable as they arose.
Elinor, though she felt really interested in the welfare of Colonel
Brandon, could not bestow all the wonder on his going so suddenly away,
which Mrs. Jennings was desirous of her feeling; for besides that the
circumstance did not in her opinion justify such lasting amazement or
variety of speculation, her wonder was otherwise disposed of. It was
engrossed by the extraordinary silence of her sister and Willoughby on
the subject, which they must know to be peculiarly interesting to them
all. As this silence continued, every day made it appear more strange
and more incompatible with the disposition of both. Why they should not
openly acknowledge to her mother and herself, what their constant
behaviour to each other declared to have taken place, Elinor could not
imagine.

She could easily conceive that marriage might not be immediately in
their power; for though Willoughby was independent, there was no reason
to believe him rich. His estate had been rated by Sir John at about six
or seven hundred a year; but he lived at an expense to which that
income could hardly be equal, and he had himself often complained of
his poverty. But for this strange kind of secrecy maintained by them
relative to their engagement, which in fact concealed nothing at all,
she could not account; and it was so wholly contradictory to their
general opinions and practice, that a doubt sometimes entered her mind
of their being really engaged, and this doubt was enough to prevent her
making any inquiry of Marianne.

Nothing could be more expressive of attachment to them all, than
Willoughby’s behaviour. To Marianne it had all the distinguishing
tenderness which a lover’s heart could give, and to the rest of the
family it was the affectionate attention of a son and a brother. The
cottage seemed to be considered and loved by him as his home; many more
of his hours were spent there than at Allenham; and if no general
engagement collected them at the park, the exercise which called him
out in the morning was almost certain of ending there, where the rest
of the day was spent by himself at the side of Marianne, and by his
favourite pointer at her feet.

One evening in particular, about a week after Colonel Brandon left the
country, his heart seemed more than usually open to every feeling of
attachment to the objects around him; and on Mrs. Dashwood’s happening
to mention her design of improving the cottage in the spring, he warmly
opposed every alteration of a place which affection had established as
perfect with him.

“What!” he exclaimed—“Improve this dear cottage! No. _That_ I will
never consent to. Not a stone must be added to its walls, not an inch
to its size, if my feelings are regarded.”

“Do not be alarmed,” said Miss Dashwood, “nothing of the kind will be
done; for my mother will never have money enough to attempt it.”

“I am heartily glad of it,” he cried. “May she always be poor, if she
can employ her riches no better.”

“Thank you, Willoughby. But you may be assured that I would not
sacrifice one sentiment of local attachment of yours, or of any one
whom I loved, for all the improvements in the world. Depend upon it
that whatever unemployed sum may remain, when I make up my accounts in
the spring, I would even rather lay it uselessly by than dispose of it
in a manner so painful to you. But are you really so attached to this
place as to see no defect in it?”

“I am,” said he. “To me it is faultless. Nay, more, I consider it as
the only form of building in which happiness is attainable, and were I
rich enough I would instantly pull Combe down, and build it up again in
the exact plan of this cottage.”

“With dark narrow stairs and a kitchen that smokes, I suppose,” said
Elinor.

“Yes,” cried he in the same eager tone, “with all and every thing
belonging to it;—in no one convenience or inconvenience about it,
should the least variation be perceptible. Then, and then only, under
such a roof, I might perhaps be as happy at Combe as I have been at
Barton.”

“I flatter myself,” replied Elinor, “that even under the disadvantage
of better rooms and a broader staircase, you will hereafter find your
own house as faultless as you now do this.”

“There certainly are circumstances,” said Willoughby, “which might
greatly endear it to me; but this place will always have one claim of
my affection, which no other can possibly share.”

Mrs. Dashwood looked with pleasure at Marianne, whose fine eyes were
fixed so expressively on Willoughby, as plainly denoted how well she
understood him.

“How often did I wish,” added he, “when I was at Allenham this time
twelvemonth, that Barton cottage were inhabited! I never passed within
view of it without admiring its situation, and grieving that no one
should live in it. How little did I then think that the very first news
I should hear from Mrs. Smith, when I next came into the country, would
be that Barton cottage was taken: and I felt an immediate satisfaction
and interest in the event, which nothing but a kind of prescience of
what happiness I should experience from it, can account for. Must it
not have been so, Marianne?” speaking to her in a lowered voice. Then
continuing his former tone, he said, “And yet this house you would
spoil, Mrs. Dashwood? You would rob it of its simplicity by imaginary
improvement! and this dear parlour in which our acquaintance first
began, and in which so many happy hours have been since spent by us
together, you would degrade to the condition of a common entrance, and
every body would be eager to pass through the room which has hitherto
contained within itself more real accommodation and comfort than any
other apartment of the handsomest dimensions in the world could
possibly afford.”

Mrs. Dashwood again assured him that no alteration of the kind should
be attempted.

“You are a good woman,” he warmly replied. “Your promise makes me easy.
Extend it a little farther, and it will make me happy. Tell me that not
only your house will remain the same, but that I shall ever find you
and yours as unchanged as your dwelling; and that you will always
consider me with the kindness which has made everything belonging to
you so dear to me.”

The promise was readily given, and Willoughby’s behaviour during the
whole of the evening declared at once his affection and happiness.

“Shall we see you tomorrow to dinner?” said Mrs. Dashwood, when he was
leaving them. “I do not ask you to come in the morning, for we must
walk to the park, to call on Lady Middleton.”

He engaged to be with them by four o’clock.

Colonel Brandon’s abrupt, unannounced departure from Barton Park had left Mrs. Jennings chattering and puzzling for three full days, her curiosity stoked so bright it rivaled the hearth fire in her parlor. There was no greater delight for the warm, gossiping old widow than parsing the comings and goings of every person in her acquaintance, and she barely paused her speculation long enough to butter her breakfast scones. She was certain no ordinary errand could have pulled the quiet, steady colonel away so fast, and ran through every possible misfortune that might have befallen him one by one, determined she would not miss the truth.
“It must be something terribly sad, that I am sure of,” she’d exclaim over her tea. “I saw it written all over his poor face. The Delaford estate never brought in more than two thousand a year, and his brother left all its accounts a tangled mess—he must have been sent for over money troubles, what else could it be? I’d give every last penny of my pin money to know the truth of it! Or wait—maybe it’s about that Miss Williams he’s always so tight-lipped about? He looked so guilty when I mentioned her the other day, didn’t he? She’s sure to be sick in town, that girl’s always been delicate as a lily. Though, no, he’s far too prudent to still be in debt over the estate… maybe his sister in Avignon has taken a turn for the worse, that would explain him riding off at such a mad dash, no time to even say proper goodbyes. Well, whatever it is, I wish him clear of all his troubles soon, and a sweet, good wife to keep him company into the bargain!”
Every new passing thought shifted her theory, and every new theory felt just as plausible as the last. Elinor, for her part, was genuinely fond of the colonel and did hope he was well, but she could not summon nearly the degree of endless, breathless speculation Mrs. Jennings pressed on her. For one thing, the colonel’s sudden trip hardly struck her as such a shocking, earth-shaking event—but far more of her wonder was occupied elsewhere, fixed on the strange, stubborn silence her sister and Willoughby maintained. They carried themselves so openly, so tenderly to each other, every glance, every lingering hand, every private laugh a declaration of their attachment, yet not a word of an engagement had crossed their lips to Mrs. Dashwood or to her. Elinor could easily guess marriage was not immediately within their power: Sir John had estimated Willoughby’s estate brought in only six or seven hundred a year, and he lived far too freely for that sum, often joking about his own empty pockets. But this total secrecy, hiding a bond that was obvious to every soul in the whole parish, made no sense at all. It was so contrary to the open, unguarded nature both Marianne and Willoughby wore so easily that sometimes a tiny, unspoken doubt crept into Elinor’s chest, and she dared not ask her sister the question burning on her tongue.
Willoughby’s devotion to the whole Dashwood household could not have been more plain. To Marianne, he gave every bit of tender, adoring attention a smitten lover could muster, and to the rest of the family he was as warm and attentive as a beloved son or brother. Barton Cottage had become more of a home to him than Allenham ever was: he spent far more hours of his days there than at his own relative’s estate, and if there was no planned dinner at the Park to draw them away, every morning walk he set out on would end at the cottage threshold, where he would sit at Marianne’s side for the rest of the afternoon while his shaggy, favorite pointer napped contentedly at her feet.
One evening, a full week after Colonel Brandon had left the county, he seemed softer, more open than ever, brimming with affection for every little thing in the small, cozy cottage. When Mrs. Dashwood casually mentioned she had planned to make small improvements to the house come spring, fixing wobbly sills and patching cracked plaster, he protested with such vehemence it made them all laugh.
“What!” he cried. “Improve this dear, perfect cottage? No, I will never consent to it. Not a single stone added to its walls, not an extra inch to its rooms, if you care even a little for my feelings.”
“Do not fret,” Elinor said, smiling. “No such work will ever happen. My mother will never have enough spare money to afford it.”
“Thank heaven for that,” he said, brightening. “May she always be too poor to waste money ruining a place that already holds all the happiness in the world.”
“Thank you, Willoughby,” Mrs. Dashwood laughed. “But I promise you, I would never sacrifice the attachment of you, or any person I love, for any trivial improvement. You may be sure that whatever small sum I have left over in the spring, I would far rather tuck it away unused than change this place in a way that pains you. But are you truly so fond of it that you cannot see a single flaw?”
“I am,” he said, earnest and soft. “To me, it is faultless. More than that, I think this is the only sort of house where true happiness can be found. If I were rich tomorrow, I would tear Combe House down to its foundations, and rebuild it exactly, exactly like this little cottage.”
“Even with its dark, narrow staircase and the kitchen that smokes something terrible whenever we roast a joint?” Elinor teased.
“Even that,” he agreed, eager as ever. “Not a single quirk, not a single convenience or inconvenience altered by even a hair. Then, and only then, could I be as happy at my own home as I have been here at Barton.”
“I have no doubt,” Elinor replied, “that even with better rooms and a wider staircase, you will one day find your own house just as faultless as you find this one.”
“There are circumstances that would make it very dear to me,” he said, his eyes drifting to Marianne. “But this place will always hold a claim on my heart that no other house can ever match.”
Mrs. Dashwood looked over to Marianne, whose luminous dark eyes were fixed unwaveringly on Willoughby, every line of her soft face declaring she understood every word he said perfectly.
“Do you know,” Willoughby added, “this time last year, when I was staying at Allenham, I used to ride past this empty cottage every week and wish so badly that some good, happy family would move in. I admired its little view over the valley so much, I grieved that it stood empty. I never thought then that the very first news Mrs. Smith would tell me when I came back to the country was that Barton Cottage was let! I felt such a rush of joy the moment I heard it, the only explanation can be that some part of me already knew all the happiness I would find here, didn’t it, Marianne?”
He spoke the last line in a low, soft voice only for her to hear, then turned back to the rest of the family. “And now you would spoil that perfect simplicity with your imaginary improvements! This very parlor, where we first met, where we have spent so many lovely hours together—you would turn it into a common entrance hall, when it holds more warmth and comfort than the grandest, largest drawing room in the whole world.”
Mrs. Dashwood promised him again no renovations of the sort would ever be made.
“You are the kindest woman alive,” he said, warmly. “That promise puts my whole heart at ease. Extend it just a little further, and make me perfectly happy: tell me not only that your house will stay just as it is, but that you and Elinor and Marianne will never change, that you will always welcome me here with the same kindness that has made every part of this cottage feel like mine.”
They promised him that easily, and Willoughby spent the rest of the evening glowing with open, unhidden joy and affection. As he pulled on his coat to leave later that night, Mrs. Dashwood called after him, “We shall hope to see you for dinner tomorrow, won’t we? I won’t ask you to come by in the morning—all three of us are walking over to the Park to call on Lady Middleton.”
He smiled, and bowed, and promised he would be back at Barton Cottage by four o’clock sharp.
